meta.subject: Geography
meta.title: Physical Features of India
meta.intro: The geological structure and six major physiographic divisions of India, their formation, characteristics and importance.

objectives: Explain the chapter’s major geographical concepts and processes.
Identify important locations and features on an outline map of India.
Relate physical geography to people, resources, environment and development.

blocks.text: India’s relief has developed through long geological processes. The Peninsular Plateau is an ancient and relatively stable landmass made mainly of igneous and metamorphic rocks.

The Himalayas are geologically young fold mountains. Their formation is linked to the northward movement of the Indian Plate and its collision with the Eurasian Plate, which compressed sediments and uplifted mountain ranges.
The Northern Plains are among India’s youngest landforms. They were built by thick alluvial deposits brought by the Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra and their tributaries.
The Himalayas stretch in an arc from the Indus gorge in the west to the Brahmaputra gorge in the east. They form a high mountain barrier and contain deep valleys, glaciers and fast-flowing rivers.
The Himadri or Greater Himalaya is the northernmost and highest range. It is relatively continuous, contains many of the loftiest peaks and remains snow-covered in many areas.
The Himachal or Lesser Himalaya lies south of Himadri. It includes ranges such as the Pir Panjal and Dhauladhar and valleys such as Kashmir, Kangra and Kullu.

The Shiwalik is the outermost range. It is made largely of unconsolidated sediments brought down by rivers. Longitudinal valleys between the Lesser Himalaya and Shiwalik are called duns, such as Dehradun.
The eastern hills and mountains are collectively called the Purvachal and include the Patkai, Naga, Manipur and Mizo hills.

The Northern Plains were formed by alluvial deposits of the Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra and their tributaries. Their level surface, fertile soils and water availability support intensive agriculture and dense settlement.
The Punjab Plains are formed mainly by the Indus and its tributaries; the Ganga Plains extend across northern India; the Brahmaputra Plains occur mainly in Assam.
Bhabar is a narrow, porous belt of pebbles along the foothills where streams may disappear underground. South of it, the Terai is a wet, marshy belt where streams re-emerge.
Bhangar is older alluvium found on higher terraces and often contains kankar. Khadar is newer alluvium in active floodplains, renewed by river deposits during floods.

The Peninsular Plateau is an ancient tableland composed largely of crystalline igneous and metamorphic rocks. It includes the Central Highlands north of the Narmada and the Deccan Plateau to its south.
The Central Highlands include the Malwa Plateau and adjoining uplands. The Chotanagpur Plateau is rich in minerals and is drained in part by the Damodar system.
The Deccan Plateau is roughly triangular. The Western Ghats form a relatively continuous edge along the west, while the Eastern Ghats are lower and discontinuous because rivers cut across them.
The Western Ghats are generally higher and cause orographic rainfall on their windward slopes. The Eastern Ghats run roughly parallel to the Bay of Bengal coast and are interrupted by major rivers.

The Indian Desert lies mainly west of the Aravalli Hills. It receives very little rainfall, has sandy plains and shifting dunes, and contains streams that are often seasonal. The Luni is an important river of this region.

The Western Coastal Plain lies between the Western Ghats and Arabian Sea and includes the Konkan, Kannad and Malabar sections. The Eastern Coastal Plain is generally broader and includes the Northern Circars and Coromandel Coast.
The eastern coast receives large rivers that build deltas, including the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri. The western coast has several estuaries and smaller coastal plains.
Lakshadweep consists mainly of coral islands in the Arabian Sea. The Andaman and Nicobar Islands lie in the Bay of Bengal; Barren Island is known for its active volcano.
